candidates.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
candidates.author: rsorto
candidates.storyText:
I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline.

The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04.

Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD.

To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge.

Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback":

1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge.

2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk.

3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now.

The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform.

As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable.

If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem.

Pura vida!

R.S.G.

candidates.title: Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast
candidates.author: _wesley
candidates.storyText:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

candidates.title: Tell HN: Anthropic found 36 bugs (6 CVEs) in Pion, OpenAI missed them
candidates.author: JoTurk
candidates.storyText:
We added Pion DTLS to Anthropic's OSS scanner last week (https://github.com/anthropics/oss-scanner/pull/93), and today we woke up to a report with 36 bugs, including 6 security vulnerabilities: 2 critical, 3 high, and 1 moderate. Four of them affect WebRTC.

Some of these vulnerabilities have been sitting in the codebase for over 4 years, surviving years of testing and security scans. It's funny that our inboxes are constantly spammed with AI-generated security reports from people using Codex and Claude, most of which flag pointless issues. Yet somehow, none of them caught these.

The funniest part? Anthropic also found 3 bugs that OpenAI's internal code review missed. I had asked OpenAI to review a new DTLS API since they use Pion and had a use case for it in SPED. Their review didn't flag any bugs. Anthropic found an authentication issue, a deadlock, and a TLS KeyUpdate bug (Maybe their model ignored this one because it's not a WebRTC issue). Luckily, the API hasn't been released yet. The fixes: https://github.com/pion/dtls/pull/1236

Here are the security advisories for the CVEs Anthropic found (all of them are pre-chatgpt!):

Critical: DTLS handshake signature confusion allows peer impersonation - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-7c2r-jhm9-43vf

Critical: Client authentication bypass through premature session caching - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-hhpj-h56m-9f2p

High: Client authentication bypass with shared session stores - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-cqhp-ggp7-58qj

High: Unbounded handshake cache allows remote memory exhaustion - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-jm57-r6vj-mwg9

High: Oversized RSA keys allow CPU exhaustion - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-jp25-wc3w-p9xp

Moderate: Repeated certificate verification allows CPU exhaustion - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-qpgj-64qg-5m4r

The most annoying part is that neither company's models were willing to help with verifying or filtering the bugs, so we had to manually review them one by one (Spent all day :/

candidates.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

candidates.title: Joint Evaluation : A Human + LLM + Multi-Agents Collaborative Framework for Comprehensive AI Safety (Jo.E)
candidates.abstract: Evaluating the safety and alignment of AI systems remains a critical challenge as foundation models grow increasingly sophisticated. Traditional evaluation methods rely heavily on human expert review, creating bottlenecks that cannot scale with rapid AI development. We introduce Jo.E (Joint Evaluation), a multi-agent collaborative framework that systematically coordinates large language model evaluators, specialized adversarial agents, and strategic human expert involvement for comprehensive safety assessments. Our framework employs a five-phase evaluation pipeline with explicit mechanisms for conflict resolution, severity scoring, and adaptive escalation. Through extensive experiments on GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 70B, and Phi-3-medium, we demonstrate that Jo.E achieves 94.2% detection accuracy compared to 78.3% for single LLM-as-Judge approaches and 86.1% for Agent-as-Judge baselines, while reducing human expert time by 54% compared to pure human evaluation. We provide detailed computational cost analysis, showing Jo.E processes 1,000 evaluations at $47.30 compared to $312.50 for human-only approaches. Our ablation studies reveal the contribution of each component, and failure case analysis identifies systematic blind spots in current evaluation paradigms.

candidates.title: Enhancing Medical AI Safety Through Multi-Agent Evaluation and Iterative Refinement
categories: ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology and Biomedicine
candidates.venue: ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology and Biomedicine
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential in healthcare but face critical challenges in ethical and safety compliance. We present a lightweight multi-agent refinement framework that enhances medical LLM safety through structured, iterative alignment. The system pairs DeepSeek R1 and Med-PaLM as generative models with LLaMA 3.1 and Phi-4 as evaluator agents that iteratively assess and refine responses against the American Medical Association's nine Principles (AMA-9) and a five-tier Safety Risk Assessment (SRA-5). Using 900 adversarial clinical prompts from the MedSafety-Eval subset, we measure convergence, violation reduction, and risk downgrading under a structured five-iteration refinement loop. The multi-agent pipeline reduced ethical violations by 89% and achieved a 92% risk-downgrade rate. DeepSeek R1 outperforms Med-PaLM in convergence efficiency (94.2% convergence; mean 2.34 iterations) compared with Med-PaLM (91.8% convergence; mean 2.67 iterations). Domain analyses reveal consistent gains across emergency, diagnostic, and therapeutic scenarios, while non-convergent cases highlight areas for improvement in legal and privacy domains. Our approach offers a scalable, cost-effective protocol for enhancing medical AI trustworthiness and provides a practical pathway toward regulator-aligned deployment of LLMs in clinical settings.

candidates.title: What Matters For Safety Alignment?
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study on the safety alignment capabilities. We evaluate what matters for safety alignment in LLMs and LRMs to provide essential insights for developing more secure and reliable AI systems. We systematically investigate and compare the influence of six critical intrinsic model characteristics and three external attack techniques. Our large-scale evaluation is conducted using 32 recent, popular LLMs and LRMs across thirteen distinct model families, spanning a parameter scale from 3B to 235B. The assessment leverages five established safety datasets and probes model vulnerabilities with 56 jailbreak techniques and four CoT attack strategies, resulting in 4.6M API calls. Our key empirical findings are fourfold. First, we identify the LRMs GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking, and GPT-OSS-120B as the top-three safest models, which substantiates the significant advantage of integrated reasoning and self-reflection mechanisms for robust safety alignment. Second, post-training and knowledge distillation may lead to a systematic degradation of safety alignment. We thus argue that safety must be treated as an explicit constraint or a core optimization objective during these stages, not merely subordinated to the pursuit of general capability. Third, we reveal a pronounced vulnerability: employing a CoT attack via a response prefix can elevate the attack success rate by 3.34x on average and from 0.6% to 96.3% for Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct. This critical finding underscores the safety risks inherent in text-completion interfaces and features that allow user-defined response prefixes in LLM services, highlighting an urgent need for architectural and deployment safeguards. Fourth, roleplay, prompt injection, and gradient-based search for adversarial prompts are the predominant methodologies for eliciting unaligned behaviors in modern models.

candidates.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

candidates.title: Enhancing Medical AI Safety Through Multi-Agent Evaluation and Iterative Refinement
categories: ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology and Biomedicine
candidates.venue: ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology and Biomedicine
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential in healthcare but face critical challenges in ethical and safety compliance. We present a lightweight multi-agent refinement framework that enhances medical LLM safety through structured, iterative alignment. The system pairs DeepSeek R1 and Med-PaLM as generative models with LLaMA 3.1 and Phi-4 as evaluator agents that iteratively assess and refine responses against the American Medical Association's nine Principles (AMA-9) and a five-tier Safety Risk Assessment (SRA-5). Using 900 adversarial clinical prompts from the MedSafety-Eval subset, we measure convergence, violation reduction, and risk downgrading under a structured five-iteration refinement loop. The multi-agent pipeline reduced ethical violations by 89% and achieved a 92% risk-downgrade rate. DeepSeek R1 outperforms Med-PaLM in convergence efficiency (94.2% convergence; mean 2.34 iterations) compared with Med-PaLM (91.8% convergence; mean 2.67 iterations). Domain analyses reveal consistent gains across emergency, diagnostic, and therapeutic scenarios, while non-convergent cases highlight areas for improvement in legal and privacy domains. Our approach offers a scalable, cost-effective protocol for enhancing medical AI trustworthiness and provides a practical pathway toward regulator-aligned deployment of LLMs in clinical settings.

candidates.title: Bypassing Safety Alignment via API Design: A Systematic Risk Analysis of Response Prefill in LLM Systems
candidates.abstract: Response prefill, an API feature for tasks such as structured output and continuation, exposes an unintended attack surface in large language model systems. This paper presents a cross-platform risk analysis of prefill-level jailbreaks, where attackers manipulate the initial generation state to bypass safety alignment. Unlike prompt-based attacks that rely on semantic persuasion, prefill enables direct state manipulation by injecting content into the response position before generation. We identify seven attack categories exploiting distinct behavioral and procedural vulnerabilities and implement both static template and adaptive optimization strategies. Evaluation across 14 models from 8 providers shows that adaptive strategies achieve attack success rates exceeding 99% and can amplify existing jailbreak methods by 10–15 percentage points. Token-level probability analysis reveals that prefill shifts the distribution from refusal to compliance at the initial generation phase, overwriting the model’s safety state. We demonstrate that standard input filters fail due to the semantic dependency between prompt and prefill, where harmless prefill content becomes harmful only when combined with malicious prompts. Defense evaluation shows that effective mitigation requires analyzing the joint relationship between API inputs rather than filtering components individually. We conclude that the prefill API feature can compromise safety alignment.

candidates.title: What Matters For Safety Alignment?
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study on the safety alignment capabilities. We evaluate what matters for safety alignment in LLMs and LRMs to provide essential insights for developing more secure and reliable AI systems. We systematically investigate and compare the influence of six critical intrinsic model characteristics and three external attack techniques. Our large-scale evaluation is conducted using 32 recent, popular LLMs and LRMs across thirteen distinct model families, spanning a parameter scale from 3B to 235B. The assessment leverages five established safety datasets and probes model vulnerabilities with 56 jailbreak techniques and four CoT attack strategies, resulting in 4.6M API calls. Our key empirical findings are fourfold. First, we identify the LRMs GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking, and GPT-OSS-120B as the top-three safest models, which substantiates the significant advantage of integrated reasoning and self-reflection mechanisms for robust safety alignment. Second, post-training and knowledge distillation may lead to a systematic degradation of safety alignment. We thus argue that safety must be treated as an explicit constraint or a core optimization objective during these stages, not merely subordinated to the pursuit of general capability. Third, we reveal a pronounced vulnerability: employing a CoT attack via a response prefix can elevate the attack success rate by 3.34x on average and from 0.6% to 96.3% for Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct. This critical finding underscores the safety risks inherent in text-completion interfaces and features that allow user-defined response prefixes in LLM services, highlighting an urgent need for architectural and deployment safeguards. Fourth, roleplay, prompt injection, and gradient-based search for adversarial prompts are the predominant methodologies for eliciting unaligned behaviors in modern models.

candidates.title: Joint Evaluation : A Human + LLM + Multi-Agents Collaborative Framework for Comprehensive AI Safety (Jo.E)
candidates.abstract: Evaluating the safety and alignment of AI systems remains a critical challenge as foundation models grow increasingly sophisticated. Traditional evaluation methods rely heavily on human expert review, creating bottlenecks that cannot scale with rapid AI development. We introduce Jo.E (Joint Evaluation), a multi-agent collaborative framework that systematically coordinates large language model evaluators, specialized adversarial agents, and strategic human expert involvement for comprehensive safety assessments. Our framework employs a five-phase evaluation pipeline with explicit mechanisms for conflict resolution, severity scoring, and adaptive escalation. Through extensive experiments on GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 70B, and Phi-3-medium, we demonstrate that Jo.E achieves 94.2% detection accuracy compared to 78.3% for single LLM-as-Judge approaches and 86.1% for Agent-as-Judge baselines, while reducing human expert time by 54% compared to pure human evaluation. We provide detailed computational cost analysis, showing Jo.E processes 1,000 evaluations at $47.30 compared to $312.50 for human-only approaches. Our ablation studies reveal the contribution of each component, and failure case analysis identifies systematic blind spots in current evaluation paradigms.

candidates.title: Auto-Evaluation: A Critical Measure in Driving Improvements in Quality and Safety of AI-Generated Lesson Resources
candidates.abstract: As a publicly funded body in the UK, Oak National Academy is in a unique position to innovate within this field as we have a comprehensive curriculum of approximately 13,000 open education resources (OER) for all National Curriculum subjects, designed and quality-assured by expert, human teachers. This has provided the corpus of content needed for building a high-quality AI-powered lesson planning tool, Aila, that is free to use and, therefore, accessible to all teachers across the country. Furthermore, using our evidence-informed curriculum principles, we have codified and exemplified each component of lesson design. To assess the quality of lessons produced by Aila at scale, we have developed an AI-powered auto-evaluation agent,facilitating informed improvements to enhance output quality. Through comparisons between human and auto-evaluations, we have begun to refine this agent further to increase its accuracy, measured by its alignment with an expert human evaluator. In this paper we present this iterative evaluation process through an illustrative case study focused on one quality benchmark - the level of challenge within multiple-choice quizzes. We also explore the contribution that this may make to similar projects and the wider sector.

candidates.title: Balancing Safety and Helpfulness in Healthcare AI Assistants through Iterative Preference Alignment
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in healthcare, yet ensuring their safety and trustworthiness remains a barrier to deployment. Conversational medical assistants must avoid unsafe compliance without over-refusing benign queries. We present an iterative post-deployment alignment framework that applies Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to refine models against domain-specific safety signals. Using the CARES-18K benchmark for adversarial robustness, we evaluate four LLMs (Llama-3B/8B, Meditron-8B, Mistral-7B) across multiple cycles. Our results show up to 42% improvement in safety-related metrics for harmful query detection, alongside interesting trade-offs against erroneous refusals, thereby exposing architecture-dependent calibration biases. We also perform ablation studies to identify when self-evaluation is reliable and when external or finetuned judges are necessary to maximize performance gains. Our findings underscore the importance of adopting best practices that balance patient safety, user trust, and clinical utility in the design of conversational medical assistants.

candidates.title: Anti-Regulatory AI: How "AI Safety" is Leveraged Against Regulatory Oversight
categories: Conference on Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization
candidates.venue: Conference on Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization
candidates.abstract: AI companies increasingly develop and deploy privacy-enhancing technologies, bias-constraining measures, evaluation frameworks, and alignment techniques — framing them as addressing concerns related to data privacy, algorithmic fairness, and AI safety. This paper examines the ulterior function of these technologies as mechanisms of legal influence. First, we examine how encryption, federated learning, and synthetic data — presented as enhancing privacy and reducing bias — can operate as mechanisms of avoidance with existing regulations in attempts to place data operations outside the scope of traditional regulatory frameworks. Second, we investigate how emerging AI safety practices including open-source model releases, evaluations, and alignment techniques can be used as mechanisms of change that direct regulatory focus towards industry-controlled voluntary standards and self-governance. We term this phenomenon anti-regulatory AI — the deployment of ostensibly protective technologies that simultaneously shapes the terms of regulatory oversight. Our analysis additionally reveals how technologies’ anti-regulatory functions are enabled through framing that legitimizes their deployment while obscuring their use as regulatory workarounds. This paper closes with a discussion of policy implications that centers on the consideration of business incentives that drive AI development and the role of technical expertise in assessing whether these technologies fulfill their purported protections.

candidates.title: Generative AI in Child-Robot Interaction: An Adaptive Framework with Safety and Developmental Alignment
candidates.abstract: Traditional child-robot interaction (CRI) systems constrained by scripted dialogue lack adaptability and engagement sustainability. This paper presents the GAI-CRI Adaptive Framework (GCAF), which integrates generative AI with three core components: Adaptive Cognition (real-time personalization via multimodal sensing), Developmental Alignment (age-appropriate content generation), and Ethical Safeguards (multi-layer content filtering). A controlled study with N = 42 children (M age = 9.3 years, ages 7–12) compared GCAF with scripted baselines. Results demonstrate GCAF significantly improved engagement (35.1% eye gaze increase, t(41) = 4.82, p ¡ 0.001), child-initiated interaction (41.8% more turns, t(41) = 5.23, p ¡ 0.001), and learning outcomes (184.4% gain, d = 2.20, p ¡ 0.001). Qualitative analysis identified five themes enhancing interaction quality (κ = 0.78). Safety evaluation achieved 96.2% accuracy in harmful content detection with minimal disruption. The framework demonstrates responsible GAI deployment in child-facing systems is achievable through architectural design and formal constraints.

recommendations.title: Bypassing Safety Alignment via API Design: A Systematic Risk Analysis of Response Prefill in LLM Systems
recommendations.abstract: Response prefill, an API feature for tasks such as structured output and continuation, exposes an unintended attack surface in large language model systems. This paper presents a cross-platform risk analysis of prefill-level jailbreaks, where attackers manipulate the initial generation state to bypass safety alignment. Unlike prompt-based attacks that rely on semantic persuasion, prefill enables direct state manipulation by injecting content into the response position before generation. We identify seven attack categories exploiting distinct behavioral and procedural vulnerabilities and implement both static template and adaptive optimization strategies. Evaluation across 14 models from 8 providers shows that adaptive strategies achieve attack success rates exceeding 99% and can amplify existing jailbreak methods by 10–15 percentage points. Token-level probability analysis reveals that prefill shifts the distribution from refusal to compliance at the initial generation phase, overwriting the model’s safety state. We demonstrate that standard input filters fail due to the semantic dependency between prompt and prefill, where harmless prefill content becomes harmful only when combined with malicious prompts. Defense evaluation shows that effective mitigation requires analyzing the joint relationship between API inputs rather than filtering components individually. We conclude that the prefill API feature can compromise safety alignment.

recommendations.title: What Matters For Safety Alignment?
recommendations.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study on the safety alignment capabilities. We evaluate what matters for safety alignment in LLMs and LRMs to provide essential insights for developing more secure and reliable AI systems. We systematically investigate and compare the influence of six critical intrinsic model characteristics and three external attack techniques. Our large-scale evaluation is conducted using 32 recent, popular LLMs and LRMs across thirteen distinct model families, spanning a parameter scale from 3B to 235B. The assessment leverages five established safety datasets and probes model vulnerabilities with 56 jailbreak techniques and four CoT attack strategies, resulting in 4.6M API calls. Our key empirical findings are fourfold. First, we identify the LRMs GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking, and GPT-OSS-120B as the top-three safest models, which substantiates the significant advantage of integrated reasoning and self-reflection mechanisms for robust safety alignment. Second, post-training and knowledge distillation may lead to a systematic degradation of safety alignment. We thus argue that safety must be treated as an explicit constraint or a core optimization objective during these stages, not merely subordinated to the pursuit of general capability. Third, we reveal a pronounced vulnerability: employing a CoT attack via a response prefix can elevate the attack success rate by 3.34x on average and from 0.6% to 96.3% for Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct. This critical finding underscores the safety risks inherent in text-completion interfaces and features that allow user-defined response prefixes in LLM services, highlighting an urgent need for architectural and deployment safeguards. Fourth, roleplay, prompt injection, and gradient-based search for adversarial prompts are the predominant methodologies for eliciting unaligned behaviors in modern models.

recommendations.title: Joint Evaluation : A Human + LLM + Multi-Agents Collaborative Framework for Comprehensive AI Safety (Jo.E)
recommendations.abstract: Evaluating the safety and alignment of AI systems remains a critical challenge as foundation models grow increasingly sophisticated. Traditional evaluation methods rely heavily on human expert review, creating bottlenecks that cannot scale with rapid AI development. We introduce Jo.E (Joint Evaluation), a multi-agent collaborative framework that systematically coordinates large language model evaluators, specialized adversarial agents, and strategic human expert involvement for comprehensive safety assessments. Our framework employs a five-phase evaluation pipeline with explicit mechanisms for conflict resolution, severity scoring, and adaptive escalation. Through extensive experiments on GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1 70B, and Phi-3-medium, we demonstrate that Jo.E achieves 94.2% detection accuracy compared to 78.3% for single LLM-as-Judge approaches and 86.1% for Agent-as-Judge baselines, while reducing human expert time by 54% compared to pure human evaluation. We provide detailed computational cost analysis, showing Jo.E processes 1,000 evaluations at $47.30 compared to $312.50 for human-only approaches. Our ablation studies reveal the contribution of each component, and failure case analysis identifies systematic blind spots in current evaluation paradigms.
